items.stem: What does structured concurrency guarantee for coroutines launched in a scope?

options.text: Child coroutines are tracked and cancelled with the scope, preventing leaks
options.rationale: A scope awaits and cancels its children, tying their lifetime to it.

options.text: Every coroutine runs on a separate OS thread
options.rationale: Coroutines multiplex over threads via dispatchers.

options.text: Coroutines cannot be cancelled once launched
options.rationale: Cancellation is cooperative and central to structured concurrency.

options.text: Launching on GlobalScope is the recommended default
options.rationale: GlobalScope breaks structured concurrency and risks leaks.

items.explanation: A scope awaits and cancels its children, tying their lifetime to it.

items.stem: Select TWO accurate statements about Kotlin Flows.

options.text: A cold flow does not produce values until it is collected
options.rationale: Cold flows run their producer per collector, on collection.

options.text: Flow operators such as map build a new flow lazily
options.rationale: Operators compose without running until a terminal collect.

options.text: A flow always runs its producer once at construction time
options.rationale: Cold flows run on collection, not construction.

items.explanation: Cold flows run their producer per collector, on collection.

items.stem: Why mark a higher-order function inline in performance-sensitive Kotlin code?

options.text: It inlines the lambda body at the call site, avoiding function-object allocation
options.rationale: Inlining removes the lambda object and call overhead, enabling reified generics too.

options.text: It makes the function run on a background thread
options.rationale: inline has nothing to do with threading.

options.text: It prevents the function from taking lambda arguments
options.rationale: inline is specifically useful for lambda arguments.

items.explanation: Inlining removes the lambda object and call overhead, enabling reified generics too.
